record.field: Escodoo - Rescue a failing Odoo project

div.h1: Your Odoo project stalled. It is recoverable.
div.p: We take over projects in progress, with full or partial recovery of your data and your configuration. In most cases the work already done is worth keeping — what failed was the method, not the platform.
The go-live date has moved three times and nobody can say what is actually left.
Your team went back to the spreadsheets because the system is slower than the old way.
Fiscal documents are being rejected and the answer is always that it is being looked into.
Nobody knows what was customised, because there is no repository you can read.
The supplier stopped replying, or the one person who understood the project left.
Every small change costs more than it should, and takes longer than it should.

div.h2: It starts with an assessment, not a project
div.p: Fixed scope, fixed price, one to two weeks. You get a document, and you are free to act on it with anyone.

ul.li: The installed module list, split into standard, community and proprietary custom
The quality of the custom code and how much of it duplicates something that already exists
Data integrity, especially the accounting and fiscal records
Which processes are genuinely in the system and which are still outside it
The upgrade risk your current installation carries
A written state of the installation, in language a director can read
What is worth keeping, what should be replaced by a community module and what should be deleted
A recovery plan with phases, durations and a range per phase
An honest verdict on whether restarting is cheaper than recovering, when it is

div.p: We do not need the previous supplier's cooperation, and we do not badmouth them either. A database dump and access to the server is enough to start. If there is a repository, we ask for it; if there is not, we reconstruct the module list from the running instance and put it under version control, which is usually the first thing that was missing.
If you are still deciding whether to change supplier at all, start with a second opinion instead. It is smaller, cheaper and commits you to nothing.

t.t-value: 'Tell us where the project is stuck'
'A thirty minute conversation is usually enough for us to tell you whether this is recoverable and roughly what it would take.'

div.p: Whoever upgrades best is whoever wrote the migration scripts upstream. We maintain community modules across versions, which means we have already migrated most of what is in your installation.

div.h2: The upgrade cost is spread, not charged as a shock
div.p: On our maintenance contracts the version upgrade is included in the monthly fee. You are not presented with a large invoice every few years, which is the mechanism that keeps companies stranded on old versions until a regulatory deadline forces the issue.

div.h2: Why it is no longer optional

div.p: IBS and CBS land on the current versions first. If you are on an older Odoo, a regulatory date has just become an upgrade date. What that means for you .
Community modules receive fixes on the supported versions. Behind that window, every fix becomes bespoke work you pay for alone.
Each version you skip makes the next upgrade harder, not linearly. Three versions behind is a different kind of project from one version behind.
Fixed scope and fixed price. The estimate for the upgrade itself is driven by one number: how many of your modules are not standard.

ul.li: Your installed modules split into standard, community and proprietary custom
Which custom modules can be dropped because the standard or a community module now does it
Which need rewriting, and roughly how much
The data conversion risks specific to your version jump
A duration, a range and a proposed cut-over window

ol.li: A copy of production is upgraded in an isolated environment
Custom modules are ported, reviewed and tested
Your key users validate their own processes on their own data
A rehearsal of the cut-over, measured, so the real window is a known quantity
Cut-over with a documented rollback, and us on the operation afterwards

div.p: This is also the moment to reduce what you carry forward. Standardisation during an upgrade is far cheaper than standardisation as its own project.

t.t-value: 'Tell us the version and roughly how customised the installation is. We come back with the shape of the project and a range.'

record.field: Escodoo - Move from Totvs, SAP or a legacy ERP

div.h1: Moving off Totvs, SAP or a legacy system
div.p: When to change, what carries over, what does not, and how long it really takes. Including the parts other suppliers leave out of the first conversation.

div.h2: The signals that it is time

div.p: The annual fee grows and the system does not, while every change is quoted separately.
Your operation runs on spreadsheets that sit alongside the ERP because the ERP cannot do it.
You cannot get your own data out without paying for a report.
Modules you do not use are still on the invoice, and cancelling one is a negotiation.
Nobody can explain what the customisations do, because the code is not yours to read.
Growth or a new business line needs a capability the vendor will not build.

div.h2: What migrates, and at what fidelity

ul.li: Customers, suppliers and contacts
Products, with their fiscal classification
Stock balances by location
Open receivables and payables
Chart of accounts and balances
Open sales and purchase orders
Sales history, usually summarised rather than document by document
Production history, depending on how the old system recorded it
Attachments, when the old system lets you extract them
Issued fiscal documents. They remain legally valid in the old system, and you keep read access for the retention period.
Closed accounting periods, which are brought in as balances, not as entries.
Payroll history, which belongs with the payroll provider.

div.p: Anyone promising to migrate ten years of fiscal documents into a new ERP either has not done it or is not telling you what it will cost.

Running two systems in parallel doubles the work for your team during the overlap, and a team that is already at capacity will quietly stop using one of them. We prefer a clean cut at a period boundary, with the old system kept readable.
Data quality in the old system is usually worse than anyone expects. Cleaning it is part of the project, not a surprise halfway through, and it is the phase most likely to slip.
Your contract with the current vendor may have a notice period, an early termination clause or a data extraction fee. Read it before you set a date, and tell us what it says.

t.t-value: 'Tell us the current system, your head count and your fiscal profile. We come back with what migrates, what does not, and a realistic timeline.'

div.h1: Replace proprietary customisation with community modules
div.p: Every line of custom code in your Odoo is a line somebody has to carry to the next version. The cheapest custom module is the one you delete because a reviewed community module already does it.

div.h2: Why customisation costs more than it looks

div.p: Once to build it, then again at every upgrade, forever. A community module is maintained by the community across versions at no cost to you.
Code that lives only in your repository has been read by one team. Code in a community repository has been read by dozens of people who did not want it to break their own clients.

div.h3: It locks you to a supplier
div.p: A heavily customised installation is expensive for anyone else to take over, which is exactly why some suppliers are relaxed about creating one.
This is the service where the numbers are the product. We publish them to you at the start and at the end.

ul.li: Lines of proprietary custom code
Number of modules outside the standard and community set
Models and views overridden, and how deeply
Test coverage on what stays custom
An upgrade risk score you can track over time
Replace with an existing community module where one covers it
Delete what nobody uses, which is always more than expected
Rewrite what has to stay, properly, with tests
Contribute genuinely generic work upstream, so the community maintains it from then on
Document the rest, so the next team is not guessing

div.h2: The cheapest time to do this
div.p: Together with a version upgrade . The custom modules have to be touched anyway, so deciding which ones deserve to survive costs almost nothing extra. Doing it as a standalone project is still worth it, but it is the more expensive route, and we will tell you that before you buy it.

t.t-value: 'Send us the installed module list, or give us read access. We come back with the numbers and what they mean for your next upgrade.'

div.h1: Tax reform: get your records ready first
div.p: The new taxes are being built into the localisation upstream. What is not being built for you is the state of your own product and tax records, and that is where the transition actually breaks.
Fixed scope, fixed price, a report you can act on. It is a small product, not a project.

ul.li: Product records: NCM completeness and plausibility, item by item
Fiscal operations: CFOP and CST usage against what you actually do
Tax rules configured versus tax rules applied in practice
Which of your operations change under the new model, and which do not
Your Odoo version, and whether it can receive the new taxes at all
A gap list, prioritised by fiscal risk rather than by effort
The old to new mapping for your operations
A remediation plan with an order and a range
A clear statement of whether you need a version upgrade before anything else

div.h2: If you are on an old version, this is an upgrade deadline
div.p: The new taxes arrive on the current Odoo versions first. Back-porting a fiscal change of this size to a version that is several releases behind is not a patch, it is a bespoke project with no community behind it.
The transition runs from the 2026 test rate to the end of the old system in 2033, so there is time — but the version decision is the one with a real queue in front of it. How the upgrade works .

div.h2: Why this is not a rewrite of your system
div.p: The fiscal tax model in the community localisation is generic by design: taxes, operations and their mappings are records, not code. New taxes therefore enter as new records with new rules, and the engine that calculates them does not have to be rebuilt.

That is a structural argument, not a marketing one, and it is why we are comfortable saying the platform will handle it. What we are not comfortable saying is that your configuration will handle it, because that depends on the state of your records — which is what the audit is for.
The upstream work is public. You can watch it happen in the localisation repository , which is a level of transparency no proprietary vendor can offer you.

t.t-value: 'Tell us your Odoo version, how many products you carry and which states you operate in. We come back with a scope and a price.'
